name: Time-series break detection on the water-area series

identity.method_name: BFAST and BFAST Monitor (Verbesselt et al. 2010, 2012), the Mann-Kendall trend test with Sen's slope, and the Pettitt change-point test, applied to each lake's annual water-area series
identity.core_idea: BFAST decomposes a time series into trend, seasonal, and remainder components (an additive STL-like decomposition) and then iteratively searches the trend and seasonal components for structural breaks using OLS-MOSUM/Bai-Perron-style breakpoint detection; BFAST Monitor is its online variant, which fits a stable model to a historical period and flags the first point at which new observations depart from it. Mann-Kendall is a non-parametric, rank-based test for a monotonic (not necessarily linear) trend across an ordered series, with the Theil-Sen slope giving a robust, outlier-resistant estimate of the trend's magnitude in the series' own units (hectares/year here). Pettitt's test is a non-parametric, rank-based test (built on the Mann-Whitney U statistic) for a single unknown change-point that splits a series into two segments with different means/locations, without assuming the change is a start of a monotonic trend. Applied here, all three would be run once per lake on its own 7-point annual water-area series, not on the pooled 42-row table.
identity.official_dataset_ids: None. These are statistical methods applied to the project's own derived per-lake, per-year water-area series (6 lakes x 7 years, the same numbers that populate the 42-row tabular dataset); there is no official dataset ID to cite.

fit_to_project.ground_truth_proxy_strategy: Fully unsupervised. None of the three tests requires any encroachment label, weak or strong; each operates purely on the shape of an already-computed numeric series. This sidesteps the missing-ground-truth problem entirely for the STATISTICAL question ('is there a detectable trend or break in this series'), but it does nothing to validate whether the underlying water-area numbers themselves are accurate, since that upstream question (MNDWI threshold vs Otsu vs sub-pixel fraction, item C8) is untouched by this item.
fit_to_project.input_required: A single scalar time series per lake: the annual water-area value already produced by the current pixel-counting method (or any alternative from C8). This is already fully available inside the project's existing 42-row table; no new imagery or feature engineering is required for the 7-observations-per-lake case. Only the Sentinel-1 SAR / denser-Landsat alternative discussed below would require new data acquisition.
fit_to_project.viable_with_42_rows: only-if-reframed, and the reframing makes the sample-size problem worse, not better. The 42 rows are 6 lakes x 7 years; every one of these three tests is applied per lake, independently, on its own 7-point series -- so the effective sample size for each test run is n=7, not 42. Pooling across lakes to get n=42 would violate each test's assumption of a single ordered process (six different lakes are not repeated draws of the same underlying trend) and would conflate cross-sectional differences between lakes with genuine within-lake temporal change, so it is not a valid workaround.
fit_to_project.viable_without_ground_truth: yes. All three tests are fully unsupervised statistical procedures; no labels of any kind are needed to compute a test statistic and p-value.
fit_to_project.resolution_match_20m: Not directly applicable -- this item operates on an already-aggregated scalar area value per lake-year, not on raw pixel imagery, so spatial resolution is not the binding constraint. The genuinely analogous constraint is TEMPORAL resolution (density of the series), and this is the item's central problem: BFAST's design assumes a seasonal cycle can be estimated within each year, which requires multiple sub-annual observations per year (the original BFAST work used 16-day MODIS NDVI composites, i.e. roughly 23 observations per year); the project's cadence of exactly one observation per year is incompatible with that design assumption regardless of how good the spatial resolution of each individual scene is.
fit_to_project.fixes_which_stated_limitation: Does not fix limitation (1) (only 42 rows) -- if anything it exposes, at the per-lake level, how thin 7 points really is once a formal statistical test is asked to certify a trend or break rather than a human simply eyeballing a line chart. Does not fix limitation (2) (OpenStreetMap single snapshot). Does not fix limitation (3) (no ground truth) -- it is unsupervised, so it needs no labels, but it also produces no validated truth; a statistically 'significant' break is not proof of a real-world encroachment or desilting event. It surfaces, rather than fixes, limitation (4) (one dry-season scene per year): because the series is annual and single-snapshot, any detected 'break' between two years could be an artefact of the capture date's position relative to a mid-year desilting-refill cycle, not a genuine multi-year regime change, and this item is the clearest place in the whole project to say so explicitly.
fit_to_project.handles_desilting_confound: This is the item's central test, and the honest answer is qualified: conceptually, YES in shape, but NO in statistical power at n=7. In principle, a desilting-refill event should show up as a STEP DOWN followed later by a STEP UP (Bellandur: 15.7 ha in 2019 -> 0.4 ha in 2021 -> 107.9 ha in 2025), which Pettitt's test (run once, or twice on split sub-series) could in principle locate as one or two change-points, while Mann-Kendall would show a non-monotonic, direction-reversing pattern rather than the single-direction monotonic decline that would indicate progressive encroachment. So the DESIGN LOGIC of using shape (step-and-recover vs monotonic decline) to separate the two processes is sound and is exactly the right idea. However, with only 7 annual points, a single low outlier year (2021) surrounded by two higher-value years is statistically compatible with both 'genuine temporary drainage' and 'a noisy monotonic decline with one unusually bad year' -- no test at n=7 has the power to adjudicate between these two explanations with any real confidence, and this must be stated plainly rather than papered over with a p-value. The honest, defensible alternative is that desilting-vs-encroachment discrimination at this sample size has to rely on qualitative, external corroborating evidence (desilting tender records, BBMP/KLCDA correspondence, contemporaneous news reports, before/after imagery showing construction equipment vs. bare mud), not on the output of a statistical test.
fit_to_project.handles_hyacinth_confound: No, and it cannot by construction. Break detection operates entirely on whatever area series it is handed; if that series already undercounts water because hyacinth-covered pixels are misclassified as vegetation (the current method's known failure for Bellandur/Varthur), the break test faithfully finds trends and breaks IN THE CORRUPTED SERIES, with no visibility into or correction for the upstream water/vegetation confusion. This item inherits the hyacinth confound completely rather than mitigating it.
fit_to_project.legal_traceability: None. The series being tested is the derived water-area number computed against the OpenStreetMap polygon (project_constraints.lake_boundary), which is not a legal boundary; a statistically detected break or trend in that series has no independent tie to Master Plan buffer distances, National Green Tribunal orders, Karnataka Tank Conservation and Development Authority records, or Survey of India records. It answers 'did the OSM-polygon water area change shape over time', not 'did an encroachment occur relative to a legal boundary'.
fit_to_project.temporal_granularity: This field is the crux of the whole item. Each of the 7 annual observations is a genuinely distinct, real measurement (unlike the constant OpenStreetMap building count), so nominally the input does vary year to year. But the SERIES AS SAMPLED -- one point per year, always near the same dry-season week -- radically undersamples whatever continuous process is actually happening (desilting timing, monsoon refill timing, incremental filling), so a detected 'break' between two annual points conflates a genuine multi-year regime shift with an artefact of exactly when within the year the single annual image happened to be captured relative to a short desilting or refill window. This is precisely stated limitation (4), now expressed as a violation of every one of these three tests' implicit assumption of adequate, representative sampling of the underlying process.

implementation.libraries: R: the 'bfast' CRAN package (Verbesselt et al.; functions bfast() and bfastmonitor()) is the original, most complete, and most cited implementation of both BFAST and BFAST Monitor. Python: no single mature, widely-vetted, feature-complete Python port of full BFAST exists; the 'bfast' PyPI package (github.com/gieseke/bfast) implements only BFASTmonitor, requires OpenCL, and is aimed at GPU-parallel large-scale raster processing rather than single-series analysis -- using it here would be considerable engineering overhead for a single 7-point series [verify current maintenance status]. pymannkendall (pip install pymannkendall; Hussain & Mahmud 2019, JOSS 4(39):1556, MIT licence) implements the Mann-Kendall family of tests plus Theil-Sen and seasonal Sen's slope estimators and is the natural choice for the Mann-Kendall part of this item. ruptures (pip install ruptures; Truong, Oudre & Vayatis 2018/2020, BSD-3 licence) implements a range of generic offline change-point detection algorithms (PELT, binary segmentation, window-based, kernel-based) and can approximate a Pettitt-style single change-point search, though the library's own documentation and benchmark examples are built around signals of dozens to thousands of points, not 7. A dedicated Pettitt test can be implemented directly in a few lines of numpy (it is just a rank-based U-statistic maximisation over candidate split points), or accessed via R's 'trend' package (pettitt.test); no equally mature, widely-cited standalone Python Pettitt-test package was identified in this search [uncertain].
implementation.pretrained_weights: Not applicable. All three methods are classical statistical procedures fit fresh to each series; there are no pretrained weights of any kind.
implementation.licence: bfast (R/CRAN, GPL-2 or later), pymannkendall (MIT), ruptures (BSD-3-Clause) are all open-source and usable in an academic project. Using the R 'bfast' package from a primarily Python project would require either running R separately or bridging via rpy2, a small but real added dependency-management cost.
implementation.compute_requirement: Trivial for every variant. Fitting Mann-Kendall, Sen's slope, or Pettitt's test to a 7-point series is a sub-millisecond computation on a laptop CPU; even a full BFAST decomposition-and-breakpoint search on such a short series would run in well under a second (if it could be meaningfully applied at all, which is the point of this item). No GPU is needed. The real cost in this item is not compute time, it is correctly reasoning about and disclosing each test's minimum-sample-size assumptions.
implementation.student_days: Roughly 2-3 student-days to implement and run Mann-Kendall + Sen's slope (via pymannkendall) and a from-scratch or 'trend'-package Pettitt test across all 6 lakes, including a leave-one-year-out sensitivity pass; the code itself is simple and mostly plug-and-play. An additional 1 student-day is needed to research and write a defensible explanation of why BFAST/BFAST Monitor were NOT run (or were run only as an explicitly labelled, non-valid illustrative exercise), grounded in the methods' own published minimum-data requirements, since this is exactly the kind of claim a panel will probe.

evaluation.metrics: For Mann-Kendall: the S statistic, its normalised Z-score, and the two-sided p-value, always reported together with the Theil-Sen slope (in ha/year) as the effect-size magnitude -- reporting only significance (or only slope) without the other is misleading at this sample size. For Pettitt: the U statistic, the estimated change-point year, and its associated p-value. There is no way to compute precision/recall or any accuracy metric against a 'true' break date, because no ground-truth break-date label exists for any lake; the only available metrics are the tests' own internal statistics, not external accuracy.
evaluation.validation_protocol: No conventional train/test split applies, since each test is a single hypothesis test on one fixed series, not a fitted, reusable model. The closest available protocol is a leave-one-year-out sensitivity check: re-run each test with each single year dropped in turn (n=6 after dropping one) and report whether the conclusion (a significant trend, or a candidate change-point) survives -- this is cheap, directly interpretable at this sample size, and should be treated as mandatory reporting, not optional. Leave-one-lake-out does not apply to how each test is computed (each lake's series is tested independently as its own temporal process), though results can still be compared qualitatively across the 6 lakes to see whether similar shapes recur.
evaluation.leakage_risk: The dominant risk here is not classical train/test leakage (no model is fit for reuse) but researcher-degrees-of-freedom and multiple-testing risk: running Mann-Kendall, Pettitt, and any BFAST-style pass across 6 lakes yields up to 18 individual tests, and selectively reporting only the ones that come out 'significant' without a multiple-comparisons correction (Bonferroni or false-discovery-rate adjustment) will systematically overstate how many genuine trends or breaks were found beyond chance at n=7. A second, subtler risk is confirmation/look-ahead bias: because Bellandur's 2019-2021-2025 history is already known in advance (it is stated in this project's own constraints), there is a real temptation to tune test parameters, sub-series splits, or even the choice of which alternative water-area estimate (from C8) to feed in, until the test 'finds' the known dip -- any such tuning must be disclosed if it occurs, or explicitly avoided by pre-registering the test configuration before looking at results.
evaluation.uncertainty_reporting: Mann-Kendall and Pettitt do report p-values, which are themselves a form of uncertainty statement, but both rely on asymptotic approximations to their null distributions that are known to be less reliable at very small n; Sen's slope should therefore be reported with a bootstrap or rank-based confidence interval rather than as a bare point estimate, and Pettitt's estimated change-point YEAR should be reported as a rough, low-precision indication, not a confidently pinpointed date, given the tiny series length. Neither test produces a calibrated posterior or conformal interval; both are frequentist hypothesis tests whose 'uncertainty' is entirely the p-value plus whatever bootstrap the analyst chooses to add on top.
evaluation.augmentation_honesty_risk: Not directly applicable, but there is a specific, foreseeable temptation worth flagging: interpolating additional pseudo-annual or pseudo-monthly points between the 7 real observations (e.g. via spline or linear interpolation) purely to make BFAST's seasonal-decomposition machinery technically runnable. This must never be done to manufacture eligibility for a method that the real data does not support -- any interpolation used purely for visualisation must be clearly and separately labelled as interpolation, not treated as additional evidence for a trend or break, since it would fabricate an apparently smoother, more 'seasonal-looking' series out of a process that was never actually observed at that density.

evidence.published_performance: Verbesselt et al. 2010 (Remote Sensing of Environment 114(1):106-115) developed and validated BFAST on 16-day MODIS NDVI composites (on the order of 23 observations per year) over multi-year forested study areas in south-eastern Australia, reporting robust break detection for change magnitudes >0.1 NDVI across a range of noise levels; Verbesselt et al. 2012 (the BFAST Monitor paper, Remote Sensing of Environment) is likewise built and tested on dense, sub-annual Landsat/MODIS series spanning multiple years of historical 'stable' baseline before monitoring begins [verify exact minimum-history-length figure quoted in that paper before citing a number]. For Mann-Kendall, widely repeated hydrological/environmental-statistics guidance (traceable to Gilbert 1987, 'Statistical Methods for Environmental Pollution Monitoring', and US EPA trend-monitoring guidance) recommends a minimum of roughly 8-10 observations for the test's normal approximation and power to be considered acceptable, with 4 observations cited as an absolute technical floor at very low power [verify the exact wording and figures against Gilbert 1987 or an EPA guidance document directly]. For Pettitt, a Monte Carlo simulation study (doi 10.1080/02626667.2015.1008482, Hydrological Sciences Journal 2015) reports that the test's size and power degrade substantially at small sample sizes, with the test's empirical size reported as effectively zero in some small-T configurations tested [verify the exact numeric claim against the primary paper before quoting].
evidence.study_area_of_that_work: BFAST and BFAST Monitor were developed and validated on forest-disturbance and vegetation-phenology monitoring using dense MODIS/Landsat time series over Australian and other forested landscapes -- large-area, sub-annually-sampled vegetation studies, not urban lake water-area series. The Mann-Kendall minimum-sample guidance derives from generic hydrological/water-quality trend monitoring (rainfall, streamflow, pollutant concentration series), not from satellite-derived lake-area series specifically. The Pettitt small-sample simulation study is a generic statistical Monte Carlo exercise, not a remote-sensing or lake-specific study.
evidence.applies_to_indian_urban_lakes: No direct application of BFAST, BFAST Monitor, or the Pettitt test to Bengaluru or Indian urban lake water-area series was found in this search. Mann-Kendall plus Sen's slope, however, is very widely used in Indian hydro-climatological literature (rainfall trend studies, groundwater-level trend studies, streamflow trend studies), so the statistical machinery itself is well precedented in the Indian context generally -- just not on a 7-point annual lake-water-area series, and not for Bengaluru lakes specifically [uncertain -- a targeted literature check for Bengaluru-lake-specific Mann-Kendall trend papers was not exhaustively completed].
evidence.evidence_recency: 2010 and 2012 for BFAST and BFAST Monitor respectively (pre-2020; these are the foundational primary methodological citations for this method, analogous to Otsu 1979 in item C8, and are cited here for that reason despite their age). 2015 for the Pettitt small-sample simulation study, 2018/2020 for ruptures, and 2019 for pymannkendall. The core methodological literature this item depends on for its central 'is 7 enough' question is therefore a mix of older foundational papers and more recent small-sample-behaviour studies; none of the item's central claims rests solely on pre-2020 evidence.

risk.failure_modes: The single overriding failure mode is a sample-size violation, stated plainly: with only 7 annual observations per lake, BFAST and BFAST Monitor are NOT validly applicable. Both methods are designed for and were validated on series with a real sub-annual seasonal cycle (dozens to hundreds of observations, e.g. 16-day or monthly composites over multiple years); with one observation per year there is no seasonal cycle to decompose at all, so the seasonal-component estimation step that BFAST's entire architecture depends on is structurally impossible, not merely under-powered. Running BFAST on 7 annual points and reporting its output as if it were a valid decomposition would be a straightforward methodological error. Mann-Kendall and Pettitt are technically computable at n=7 -- they will return a number without erroring -- but n=7 sits at or below the widely-cited minimum recommended sample size (roughly 8-10) at which each test's asymptotic approximation and statistical power are considered acceptable, so any resulting p-value should be treated as weak, indicative evidence at best, never as proof of a real trend or break. A further failure mode specific to this project: a single anomalous low-water year (Bellandur 2021) sitting between two higher-value years is statistically ambiguous between 'temporary engineered drainage' and 'one bad year within an otherwise noisy monotonic decline', and no test at this sample size can resolve that ambiguity.
risk.panel_defensibility: This is exactly the question the task poses, and the only defensible position is to answer it directly rather than hedge: state plainly that BFAST/BFAST Monitor were not run as valid analyses because 7 annual points supply no seasonal cycle and fall far short of every published minimum-data guideline for these methods; state that Mann-Kendall and Pettitt were run and are technically computable at n=7 but sit at or below their own commonly cited minimum-n thresholds, so their p-values are reported as indicative/descriptive only, accompanied by a mandatory leave-one-year-out sensitivity check and the Sen's-slope magnitude alongside significance; and state that the desilting-vs-encroachment distinction for any single lake ultimately rests on qualitative, external evidence (desilting records, contemporaneous reporting) rather than on any of these tests' p-values, because no test at n=7 has the power to make that call statistically. A panel that pushes on 'is this result real' should be met with the honest minimum-sample-size figures above, not a confident-sounding but unsupportable p-value.
risk.honest_expectation: At the current annual cadence, no formal break-detection or trend test in this item can be trusted to reliably distinguish a desilting-refill cycle from a genuine progressive decline; the realistic, defensible use of Mann-Kendall and Pettitt here is as heavily caveated DESCRIPTIVE diagnostics (report the Z/p-value and Sen's slope, and the Pettitt candidate change-point year, explicitly labelled 'indicative only, n=7'), presented alongside a plain narrative account of what is independently known to have happened (e.g., Bellandur's documented desilting and refill dates) rather than as statistical proof of anything. BFAST and BFAST Monitor should not be run and presented as valid results at all under the current data.

verdict.recommended_rank: adopt-if-time for Mann-Kendall with Sen's slope and the Pettitt test, run and reported explicitly as low-power, indicative-only diagnostics with a leave-one-year-out sensitivity check; reject BFAST and BFAST Monitor outright at the current one-observation-per-year cadence, since they are not validly applicable and should not be run and reported as if they were; consider-with-reasons the Sentinel-1 SAR (or denser Landsat) upgrade path as the correct structural fix, since it is what actually resolves the 'is n=7 enough' problem rather than working around it. Sentinel-1's C-band SAR (operating since 2014, cloud- and light-independent) covers this tile at roughly a 12-day repeat cycle over India even in the current single-satellite configuration (Sentinel-1B failed in December 2021, and India was already outside the 6-day dual-satellite priority zone, so the effective revisit for this area has been on the order of 12 days for most of the study period) [verify exact per-tile acquisition counts against the actual Sentinel-1 archive for MGRS-43PGQ before committing to a number], which would yield roughly 25-30 usable acquisitions per year, or on the order of 175-210 over the 2019-2025 window -- comfortably enough to build monthly or even bi-weekly composites, giving both Mann-Kendall/Pettitt genuine statistical power (n in the tens to hundreds instead of 7) and BFAST/BFAST Monitor a real sub-annual seasonal cycle to decompose for the first time. This upgrade also directly removes the single-annual-snapshot timing problem (stated limitation 4), though it introduces its own new engineering burden -- SAR speckle filtering, incidence-angle correction, and a backscatter-based water threshold that reintroduces essentially the same Otsu/adaptive-thresholding problem discussed in item C8, now for SAR backscatter instead of MNDWI.
verdict.one_line_for_the_guide: We ran Mann-Kendall/Sen's slope and Pettitt's test on each lake's 7-year water-area series and report them as indicative-only diagnostics given the small sample size, we did not run BFAST because it needs a dense sub-annual seasonal cycle our one-scene-per-year data cannot provide, and we note that moving to Sentinel-1 SAR's roughly 12-day repeat cycle would supply enough observations per year to make all of these tests genuinely statistically valid in future work.
